newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania says Greek-based plot behind uprising.
newsitem.headline: Albania says Greek-based plot behind uprising.

text.p: Albania's secret police chief accused groups in neighbouring Greece on Wednesday of plotting to "liberate" southern Albania and said this was behind the insurrection in the border region.

Bashkim Gazidede told parliament that a plot called "Lotos" had been worked out by groups in Greece in 1990, when 45 years of rigid communist rule collapsed in Albania and the country was in upheaval.
The state-run ATA news agency reported that Gazidede said several Greek associations were involved in the plot, and were operating out of Greece, the United States and other countries.
Gazidede named numerous people, including former Albanian army officers and Greek-Americans, who, he said, were involved in or were running the "Lotos" operation.
"Lotos" was drafted in Greece and covered "the liberation of Northern Epirus from Albanian domination through an armed insurrection", he said.
The "Lotos" plan had not been realised in 1990 but was now being implemented point by point, he said. Armed rebels seized much of south Albania this month in a popular uprising.
They control most of the south and have taken huge stocks of weapons from army munitions depots. The rebels have refused to surrender their arms until President Sali Berisha resigns.
So far they have made no calls for autonomy or separation from Albania. At one point they threatened to set up a rival government to oppose Berisha but they never carried this out.
A large ethnic Greek minority, estimated at 60,000 to 120,000 people, lives in southern Albania and has caused friction between the two Balkan neighbours in the past.
Albania lodged a protest this month when Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Yannos Kranidiotis crossed the border to visit rebel heaquarters in the town of Gjirokaster.
Greeks refer to southern Albania as "Northern Epirus" and it sits just across the border from Greece's "Southern Epirus" region.
The economies of the two regions have become closely linked and the Greek drachma is used freely on the Albanian side of the border.
Gazidede named a number of people both inside and outside Albania who, he said, were part of the "Lotos" plan and were still working to separate the southern Albanian region.
